title: Medieval close: a mirror
hook: every age of saints shows what that age most needed

segments.voice: Yesterday, cockle, the weeds that grew beside the wheat in one field. Your line was both are true. Where did you add the other half? Today closes the middle ages. Day eight hundred forty-six.

Hold up a mirror to a room and it shows you the room. Not an idea of it. What's actually there, including what's missing: the empty chair, the bare wall. For a long stretch now we've walked through the middle ages, from a monastery bell to a stripped abbey roof. Today we hold up a mirror to the whole stretch, and the mirror is the saints. Today's word: mirror.
screen: `A MIRROR SHOWS THE ROOM.` → `INCLUDING WHAT'S MISSING.` → `THE SAINTS AS A MIRROR.`

segments.voice: Here's one way to read them: each age's saints show what that age was short of. First, violence. In an age of private wars and crusades, we met the Peace of God, Louis the king doing justice under an oak, and Francis walking unarmed to a sultan. Peace was what was missing, so peacemakers shone. Second, ignorance and confusion. The universities rose, Thomas the dumb ox reasoned his way toward God, and Bonaventure mapped a journey of the mind. When the popes lived away from Rome, a dyer's daughter, Catherine, told one to go home. Third, suffering. When plague came, Julian, walled in beside her church, heard that all shall be well, and saw all that is made, as small as a hazelnut in her hand. Elizabeth and Catherine of Genoa nursed the sick. Fourth, power and greed. When popes grew worldly and empires reached for gold, Las Casas changed, a pope wrote that the peoples of the Americas are truly human, Juan Diego the little one carried flowers to a bishop, and Fisher refused a king. Mirrors don't flatter. Paul says, in the Douay-Rheims: "We see now through a glass in a dark manner; but then face to face." Looking back, we see these centuries through a glass too: partly, darkly, with our own reflection in the frame. And Jesus once told some questioners who could read the sky that they could not read "the signs of the times." That's the harder question this block leaves behind. Not what did their age need. What does ours?
screen: `AN AGE OF VIOLENCE: PEACEMAKERS.` · `AN AGE OF CONFUSION: TEACHERS.` · `AN AGE OF PLAGUE: HEALERS.` · `AN AGE OF GREED: THOSE WHO CHANGED.` · then, large: `THE SIGNS OF THE TIMES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: ask what your age needs. Sit, and breathe. Look around your own time the way we've looked at theirs: your city, your news, your group chats, your family. Ask quietly, what is missing here? What kind of person would shine, simply by being the opposite of what's wrong? Don't rush to an answer. Let one come. If you pray, you can ask to be shown it. If you don't, just keep the question open until the bell. The bell holds the time.
Mirror. The image for this look back at the middle ages, where the saints show what each age was missing, and now ask what ours is short of. Today's word.

Your line: what does my age need. Today, ask it once of someone you trust, and listen to their answer before giving yours. Tomorrow a new block begins, reform, mission and revolution, with a soldier hit by a cannonball. Day eight hundred forty-six.

howItsDone: Catholics read the lives of the saints through the year, keeping their feasts in the Church's calendar; homilies and spiritual reading often ask what a saint's life says to the present day.

notes: Block C close (days 797–846): the teach names figures from earlier days (Peace of God, Louis IX, Francis and the sultan, the universities, Aquinas, Bonaventure, Catherine of Siena and Avignon, Julian, Elizabeth, Catherine of Genoa, Las Casas, Sublimis Deus, Juan Diego, Fisher). Assumes those days follow their index lines. Louis IX 'doing justice under an oak' (Joinville) is a detail; confirm or cut.
The index's 'every age of saints shows what that age most needed' is softened to 'one way to read them: each age's saints show what that age was short of'.

Avignon and the Schism are presented together ('when popes left Rome and rivals split the Church'); Catherine urged the return from Avignon, before the Schism. Confirm the phrasing doesn't imply she resolved the Schism.
Confirm Douay-Rheims wording of 1 Corinthians 13:12 and Matthew 16:3 ('the signs of the times').
Next block (Block D: Reform, mission and revolution) begins with day 847, Pamplona.
